children: Starting a new home or replacing old cookers and cookware could get costlier for Indian households as kitchenware makers grapple with higher input costs. The pressure comes at a time when demand for premium cookware, including triply products, is gaining traction, even as manufacturers remain dependent on imports for key raw materials.

Aluminium prices have risen by more than 50 per cent, with only a partial correction of around 10 per cent, said Rajendra Gandhi, Managing Director of Stovekraft, which sells kitchenware under the Pigeon and Gilma brands. “There is no meaningful reduction in cost,” he said in a post-quarter analyst call, adding that the company had seen severe margin pressure as input costs increased.

Gandhi said consumers were shifting from aluminium pressure cookers to alternatives such as stainless steel and triply products. While the company follows a cost-plus model and would adjust prices in response to further cost changes, the correction in aluminium prices so far was not enough to offset the increase, he said.

The pressure extends beyond metals. TTK Prestige said nearly 95 per cent of its input-cost line items had been affected, including packaging materials, handles, rubber-related and chemical inputs. Managing Director and CEO Venkatesh Vijayaraghavan said price increases across the industry had been staggered and that manufacturers had not fully absorbed the higher costs. Further cost increases would need to be mitigated over the coming quarters, he said.

The cost pressure is particularly relevant for triply cookware, one of the industry’s faster-growing segments. TTK Prestige said triply products, which combine stainless steel and aluminium, were growing at around 1.5 times the industry’s average rate. However, triply circles, circular discs that combine stainless steel on the outside, aluminium at the core, and magnetic steel on the outside, are imported, with no domestic production at present. China is among the dominant sources, Vijayaraghavan said.

Stovekraft is looking to secure supplies through backward integration. The company plans to invest 20 million Chinese yuan, or around ₹29-30 crore, in its China operations to manufacture triply circles used in pressure cookers and cookware. Gandhi said the investment was aimed at mitigating supply-chain risks and improving cost efficiency. The brownfield facility was expected to begin manufacturing by December-end or early January.

title: Kitchenware makers caught between rising costs and price-sensitive consumers
